title: Estimated risk for altered fetal growth resulting from exposure to fine particles during pregnancy: an epidemiologic prospective cohort study in Poland.
ehr_evidence: After participating women had given birth, maternal and child hospital records were reviewed to obtain data on complications of delivery; exposure was measured by personal environmental monitoring sampler (PEMS) over 48 hr during the second trimester and data on demographics, house characteristics, and reproductive history were collected via questionnaires.
summary: A prospective community-based cohort study of 362 nonsmoking pregnant women in Krakow, Poland, examining the effect of personal PM2.5 exposure during pregnancy on birth weight, length, and head circumference.
key_findings: The regression model explained 33.4% of the variability in birth weight (β = –200.8, p = 0.03).
PM2.5 was significantly associated with shorter birth length (β = –1.44, p = 0.01) and smaller head circumference (β = –0.73, p = 0.02).
Newborns of mothers with higher PM2.5 exposure (above the median of 36.3 µg/m3) had shorter length at birth by 0.9 cm, with reductions in HC of 0.3 cm and birth weight of 128.3 g.
An increase in PM2.5 exposure from 10 to 50 µg/m3 was predicted to reduce birth weight by 140.3 g, birth length by 1.0 cm, and HC by 0.5 cm.
The effect of environmental tobacco smoke (ETS) was insignificant in all regression models.
No significant association was found between PM2.5 or ETS and shortened gestational age.
pathologies_diseases: adverse fetal growth (reduced birth weight, length, and head circumference)
population: 362 nonsmoking women with singleton pregnancies, aged 18-35, free from chronic diseases such as diabetes and hypertension, attending prenatal clinics in Krakow, Poland, giving birth between 34 and 42-43 weeks of gestation (2001-2003)
exposure_domain: air pollution (personal fine particulate matter PM2.5)
limitations: Personal exposure to PM2.5 was measured over only a short 48-hr period in the second trimester.
ETS and PM2.5 were significantly correlated, making it difficult to separate their effects.
ETS exposure was self-reported and may be subject to underestimation bias.
PM2.5 may act as a proxy for a complex mixture of other toxic agents (e.g., PAHs).
